vectors.enisa_quote: into space operations contorl systems and/or satellite data receivers and trasmitters
vectors.reason: Malware is placed into operations control systems and data receivers/transmitters on the ground.

vectors.enisa_quote: Malicious code could also be injected into software updates
vectors.reason: Injection into software updates and patches is a delivery path through the update/supply pipeline.

rows.reason: Suppressing FDIR is not part of ENISA's injection of rootkits, backdoors or update payloads.
Disrupting the telemetry chain is not what ENISA's malicious injection describes.
Inhibiting ground telemetry rendering is not described; ENISA names injected software, not ground-side denial.
Jamming the downlink is the defining behaviour of TR44 and has nothing to do with injected code.
Suppressing telemetry at the source is not an outcome ENISA states for injection.
Falsifying housekeeping values is not stated; hiding is covered here only by the rootkit/bootkit rows.
Changing telemetry downlink modes is not mentioned in the injection text.
Biasing the on-board clock is not described by ENISA.
GPS ephemeris deception is a spoofing effect, not injection of software.
Safe-mode abuse is not part of the ENISA description.
Editing a whitelist is not named; ENISA lists rootkits, bootkits and backdoors only.

rows.sparta_quote: A rootkit hides malicious activity by interposing on reporting paths after the system has booted
rows.reason: The injected rootkit named by ENISA conceals itself through runtime hooks of reporting paths.

rows.sparta_quote: A bootkit hides activity by running first and shaping what higher layers will later observe
rows.reason: The injected bootkit named by ENISA hides activity from early boot.
Deceiving on-board SSA sensors is a spoofing matter, unrelated to injected software.
Geofence- or time-gated triggering of malware is not described; ENISA lists rootkits, bootkits and backdoors and says nothing about trigger conditions.
Corrupting firmware or hardware logic is the defining behaviour of TR42, not of code injection.
Exploiting hardware design errata injects no code and ENISA does not mention it.
Direct hardware or sector commands that corrupt non-volatile stores are covered by TR42 firmware corruption.
Abusing code flaws is the software-exploit threat TR48; ENISA here describes planting code, not exploiting a bug.
Exploiting flight-software flaws is TR48's software-exploit behaviour, not the planting of malware described here.
Exploiting OS primitives is TR48's software-exploit behaviour, not a malicious injection.
Using known COTS/FOSS defects is TR48's vulnerability exploitation; ENISA here names injection.

rows.enisa_quote: Injection of malicious software (e.g. rootkits, bootkits, backdoors)
rows.sparta_quote: introducing executable logic that runs on the vehicle
rows.reason: Malicious Code is the technique ENISA names: software injected into control systems and receivers/transmitters.
Ransomware is not listed; ENISA's examples are rootkits, bootkits and backdoors.
A wiper is the destructive-malware example under third-party non-compliance (TR26); ENISA's injection stresses extraction and manipulation.

rows.sparta_quote: A rootkit hides the presence and activity of other malicious components
rows.reason: ENISA lists rootkits as an injected software type.

rows.sparta_quote: A bootkit positions itself in the pre-OS boot chain
rows.reason: ENISA lists bootkits as an injected software type.
ENISA names the threat 'injection' of malicious software; injecting code into running trusted onboard processes is the on-board form of that injection, kept next to the direct-memory-write route.
rows.sparta_quote: inject malicious code into trusted onboard software processes

Transponder remapping is not described by ENISA.

review_response.finding: EX-0010.05 On-Board Process Injection dropped although the threat is called injection (major).
review_response.action: fixed: kept as K-ACTION execution; ENISA's 'Injection of malicious software' into control systems and receivers/transmitters is described by SPARTA EX-0010.05 as injecting code into trusted onboard processes.

review_response.finding: IA-0001.02 and IA-0007.01 are two keeps for the same clause but coded K-ENABLE vs K-ACTION (minor).
review_response.action: fixed: both K-ENABLE, role entry, enabling EX-0010, same wording, same reason structure; they differ only by vector (supplier vs operator pipeline).

review_response.finding: PER-0001 -> TR48 weakens the bootkit chain (minor).
review_response.action: fixed: PER-0001 is D-UNDESCRIBED (no D-OTHER to TR48). Residency of the bootkit is carried by EX-0010.04 and backdoor persistence by PER-0002/PER-0002.02.

review_response.finding: EXF-0010 only fits the payload half of 'bus or payload' (minor).
review_response.action: kept because: no SPARTA exfiltration technique fits bus-side extraction by implanted code; EXF-0010 is the nearest and its text names implanted payload code.

review_response.finding: IMP-0012 is kept by seven threats and does not discriminate (minor).
review_response.action: kept because: ENISA's 'affecting ... on-orbit software updates, upgrades, patches' is exactly a change of the implementation (SPARTA IMP-0012); the overlap reflects SPARTA, which has no finer impact technique for altered software.

review_response.finding: Process commentary in reasons / re-pointed D-OTHER (EX-0014.04), review_arch patterns 2, 4, 6.
review_response.action: fixed: EX-0014.04 reason rewritten; D-OTHER rows re-checked against the current keeps of their target threats.
fixed: the rootkit EX-0010.03 enables its concealment DE-0007 and the bootkit EX-0010.04 enables DE-0008.

review_response.finding: m7: EX-0010.05 kept on the word 'injection'
